newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian 10-yr OLO yield seen breaking 6.00 pct.
newsitem.headline: Belgian 10-yr OLO yield seen breaking 6.00 pct.

text.p: The yield on benchmark Belgian 10-year OLOs was seen breaking through 6.00 percent for the first time ever on Wednesday if U.S. producer price data allayed fears of a U.S. rate rise.

But OLO dealers expected the Belgian market to continue to lag Germany in the near term as worries over European economic and monetary union (EMU) and the dollar drove money into Deutsche mark-denominated paper.
With the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) due to meet late in the European session trade would also likely be quiet, they said.
The yield on the May 2006 OLO ended at 6.02 percent on Tuesday, down from 6.06 percent late on Friday. The market was closed Monday for Remebrance Day.
The spread over Bunds widened to 17 from 14 basis points.
"Belgium won't go through 6.00 percent on its own. There's not one single buyer in this market. The domestics are sleeping," said a trader at a foreign domestic primary dealer.
"It will trade up on the back of Bunds, but the spread will only tighten if Bunds collapse," he said.

This trader said Germany's recent tough talk on EMU was a signal for the market that recent convergence trades had gone too far. "The Bundesbank does not like seeing countries like Belgium and France trading through Bunds," he said, noting most Belgian maturities still trade at a discount to Bunds.

After the OLO market had wound down on Tuesday, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said countries must honestly meet the economic criteria for monetary union. He also called for European Union finance ministers to agree a post-EMU fiscal stability pact after they failed to do so at a meeting on Monday.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell warned its clients on Tuesday that the risk EMU did not now happen at all or on time had risen to 45 percent from 30 percent previously.
Dealers said the flight to quality pitched German Bobls higher, and this in turn pulled up shorter dated Belgian maturities, steepening the curve.
The exception was the five year area of the curve, where there was some selling pressure in favour of Dutch paper, one trader said. Another said the move had not been pronounced.
